sections.html:
The city lies in the far southwest of Utah within Washington County, a few miles east of St. George off Interstate 15, at roughly 2,894 feet. Its population was 18,761 in 2010 and 27,993 in 2020, and the July 2025 estimate at the top of this page is 37,107. Only St. George is bigger in the county.

Streets near the original townsite feel nothing like the planned subdivisions added after 2000, so the buyer pool differs by neighborhood. Growth began in the 1980s and then accelerated, which explains why a lot of houses here are less than twenty-five years old.

Second homes explain part of the vacancy. The county water district says they exceed 20% of homes in Washington County.

sections.h2: Desert heat and what buyers inspect
sections.html:
This is a hot, dry desert city, so roofs, cooling systems and exterior finishes wear fastest. St. George, in the same valley, averages a 101.9 degree July high and a 28.4 degree January low, and its record of 118 degrees came on July 4, 2007.

Expect a buyer's walk-through to focus on:

  • How old the air conditioner is and how well it works, since it runs for months.
  • Whether roof underlayment and tile or shingles have held up to years of sun.
  • Stucco cracks, faded paint and sun damage on south-facing walls and decks.
  • Irrigation lines and pool equipment, which break more often in extreme heat.

Put-off repairs here are a common reason listings linger, and a common reason owners consider an as-is sale where the buyer accepts the house in its current condition.

Water limits what a yard here can look like. Washington County's towns draw on the Virgin River basin and already use over 90% of its dependable yearly supply, so the rules keep tightening.

Most cities now limit turf on new residential lots to 8% of the lot area, with a separate limit on large lots. Turf is not allowed in park strips, in strips under 8 feet wide, or on slopes. Where secondary or reuse water exists, developers must use it for irrigation. Watering with drinking water is off limits between 10 a.m. and 8 p.m. in summer, and heavy users above a monthly volume pay an excessive water use fee of $1.00 per 1,000 gallons.

Before you rip out or replant a yard, look at the city's water conservation form. On an older lot, a big lawn means a bigger water bill, and buyers notice.

The city has three Interstate 15 exits. Exit 13 is billed as the gateway to the county and anchors the Green Springs master-planned community, a hospital and an auto mall. Near Exit 10 you will find a Walmart Supercenter, The Home Depot, Kohl's, Best Buy, Albertsons and In-N-Out, per a 2022 retail profile prepared for the city.

That profile also counts more than 3,300 homes added from 2017 through 2021, some of them denser multifamily buildings near Exit 13. A resale house competes with all of that new supply, so price with it in mind. Washington belongs to the Washington County School District, and families will want to know which school your address feeds. Get the boundary confirmed before you advertise.

sections.h2: Permits and city rules before you sell
sections.html:
Anything you build or finish before listing should be permitted. In Washington City the Building Department covers single-family permits, additions, basement finishes, demolition, detached accessory buildings, garages and shops, sheds and patio covers, pools and solar.

  • Permit applications and inspection requests go through the City Inspect portal. A request submitted by 5 p.m. on a business day is typically handled the following business day.
  • Work hours are 6 a.m. to 10 p.m. Concrete crews may begin at 3 a.m. between April and October.
  • An accessory dwelling unit may require a deed restriction.
  • Visit the department at 111 North 100 East or call (435) 656-6326.

A buyer's inspector often spots unpermitted work such as a finished basement. If you are unsure what a past owner did, ask the department before you list.

sections.h2: Property tax and recording when you sell
sections.html:
Washington County collects real property tax once a year, with payment due November 30. The bill attaches to the parcel rather than to you, so an unpaid balance travels with the house to the next owner. The Treasurer mails each owner a notice, and the title company splits the year's bill between you and the buyer at closing. The Treasurer takes partial payments of $10 or more per parcel at any time, but there are no payment plans for delinquent balances. After five years or more of delinquency, a parcel can be offered at the county tax sale each May.

Utah applies a 45% residential exemption, so a home you live in is assessed on 55% of market value. A second home or a vacant house gets no exemption and is assessed at full value. If you moved out and kept the house, look at your bill before you list.

The Washington County Recorder, at 111 East Tabernacle Street in St. George, records the deed. Expect $45.00 per document and $2.00 for each legal description past the tenth. The office stops accepting recordings at 4:45 p.m. Mountain Time.

sections.h2: Ways to sell a Washington house
sections.html:
Three routes are open to you: hire an agent, sell without one, or take a cash offer from an investor. Each swaps speed, price and effort differently. An agent listing reaches the most buyers, though you will live through showings, inspection requests and a closing date tied to the buyer's mortgage approval.

Cash fits when the house needs work, when a move is coming, or when you inherited property here and would rather not manage it. Cash Home Buyers makes offers on houses in any condition, and asking for one does not commit you. There are no showings, no appraisal delays and little repair haggling, and you pick the closing date that suits you.

A handful of issues come up again and again with Washington sellers.

  • Sun-baked roofs, stucco and air conditioners that buyers will discount.
  • Out-of-state heirs who now own a Washington County house.
  • Second-home owners surprised by full-value taxation.
  • New construction near Exit 13 and the Washington Fields area pulling buyers away from resale houses.
  • Unpermitted or half-finished projects that turn up in an inspection.

Whichever applies, begin by pulling together the deed, your latest tax notice and any permit records. Buyers, title companies and cash buyers all ask for those first.

faqs.q: Is Washington, UT the same as Washington County?
faqs.a: No. Washington is a city, and Washington County is the county that contains it along with St. George, Hurricane and other communities. Property tax bills and deeds in the city go through county offices in St. George.

faqs.q: When are property taxes due in Washington, Utah?
faqs.a: Real property taxes are due November 30 each year. The County Treasurer mails the notice, and if you never receive one you are still responsible for the bill. The Treasurer's Office can send a copy on request.

faqs.q: How much does it cost to record a deed in Washington County?
faqs.a: The fee is $45.00 per document, plus $2.00 for each legal description over ten. Recordings are not accepted after 4:45 p.m. Mountain Time.

faqs.q: Do I need a permit for work on my Washington house?
faqs.a: Usually yes for additions, basement finishes, pools, solar and detached buildings. Washington City's Building Department issues permits through its City Inspect portal. Call (435) 656-6326 if you are not sure.

faqs.q: Can I sell a Washington house that needs repairs?
faqs.a: Yes. Houses are sold in any condition, and an as-is sale to a cash buyer is one way to avoid paying for repairs first.
